title: The seventh rank

D0.outcome: Explains why a rook on the seventh attacks pawns from behind and confines the king, and that this is strongest when the rank is protected and the king is cut off.

D1.outcome: Told to invade the seventh, finds the entry square and the targets on the rank (pawns, fork squares).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to invade now, double the rooks first, or not at all; notices a fork on the seventh.

D3.outcome: Tells apart the special cases (king cut off with an advanced passer, two rooks giving perpetual check, rook and knight apparatus) and checks that the rank is really absolute before counting on a win.

misconceptions: A rook on the seventh rank is always winning.
Any route to the seventh counts as using the file.
conditions: The enemy is cramped on the rank, has few defenders there, and the way in is safe.
The rank is 'absolute' only if the enemy king is confined behind it (with an advanced passer, wins almost always).
contrasts: A rook on the seventh while the king can step out is only a draw.
A catastrophic invasion arises from the opponent's serious mistakes; in normal play the seventh is mostly an endgame asset.
A rook on the seventh rank with nothing there to attack.
